Good morning, members of EUCS. Very happy to be here as we are excited to be introducing the updated climate action strategy for the city of Saskatoon. Next slide, please.
The opportunity has been committed to climate action through the global covenant of mayors for climate and energy since 2015.
To meet those commitments, we developed the low emissions community plan and the corporate climate adaptation strategy in 2019.
Then, in 2023, Council adopted an updated greenhouse gas reduction target of net zero by 2050 and noted that a community climate adaptation plan was still needed.
We have developed an updated climate action strategy. Next slide, please.
The climate action strategy is grounded in evidence shaped by local voices and focuses on practical and achievable actions that support economic resilience and quality of life.

The strategy is made up of two playbooks. These include the net zero transformation playbook, which outlines the measures that reduce carbon pollution and the climate resilience playbook, which outlines our efforts to prepare the community to become more resilient to the impacts of a changing climate.
The playbook actions are guided by commitment to equity, reconciliation, prosperity, and meopomotsoin, or the good life.
The strategy demonstrates how decisive steps now will help create a safer, healthier, and more prosperous Saskatoon.
Next slide, climate action relates to many areas of community life and across these areas the city has varying degrees of control.
The strategy outlines levers for how the city can influence, enable, or directly implement change locally and with our own operations.
These levers provide a systematic approach to driving change.
For example, we have little control of our purchases that residents make, but can use education or incentives to guide their behavior.
Meanwhile, the city has full control over our own operations and infrastructure and assets that we purchase. Next slide, please.

Getting into the details of the strategy, we start with the net zero transformation playbook, which consists of seven goals to first reduce and then once all other measures have been implemented remove carbon.
Next slide, please.
The actions in the net zero playbook aim to keep Saskatoon safe, healthy, and prosperous.
Some examples are shown on the slide. Next slide, please.
I've got an animation here.
As shown, electrifying vehicles and investing in renewables help keep Saskatoon safe and healthy by improving our air quality while developing local reuse markets help us support local economies.
Next slide, please.
The development of the net zero playbook was supported by GHG greenhouse gas modeling to help prioritize actions and understand gaps in achieving targets.
This graph shows community emissions until 2050.
So if you look at the black line, these are at actual historical emissions up to 2023, then the red line shows expected emissions if no action was taken.
And the blue shows the modeled climate action pathway, including all quantifiable actions from the climate action strategy.
Because the carbon intensity of electricity grid is a critical but uncertain factor influencing our ability to achieve our carbon reduction targets, we modeled several grid sensitivities.
The one shown here assumes that Sask power achieves their state-stated target of a carbon neutral electricity grid by 2050, but with minimal improvements in the near term.
You may notice that the blue model climate action scenario does not reach the net zero by 2050 target.

This means that while we understand our near term actions and can significantly progress climate action and carbon reductions over the next decade by following the actions in the playbook, there is further work to scope and accurately quantify later actions to meet longer term climate targets.
Later actions will be more clearly and accurately established in future strategies alongside technical advancements as they become available.
Next slide please. Switching over to our climate resilience playbook, the actions were developed by first updating climate hazard projections for Saskatoon.

In summary, we can expect more very hot days and longer heatways, more days with heavy wildfire smoke, unpredictable rainfall drought and flooding, and more severe and frequent extreme weather. Next slide.

A climate risk assessment was carried out with stakeholders across city departments and the community, which helped us identify the top rated climate risk to Saskatoon, including in part, unsafe indoor air temperatures during heat events, damage to and loss of the tree canopy, widespread and localized loss of power, health and safety risk from severe winter weather and reduced acting to housing caused by physical damage and increasing demand being exasperated by climate change.
Next slide. The climate resilience playbook seeks to address these climate risks and hazards to prepare the city and the community. It has six key goals as shown on this slide.
Next slide. These key resilience building actions also aim to keep Saskatoon safe, healthy and prosperous.
Key resilience building actions are shown on this slide, and you can switch the slide, and they include integrating climate risk and adaptation into asset management process and practices,

conserving, restoring, growing and managing natural infrastructure to mitigate the impacts of climate hazards like heat and providing financing and incentives for climate resilience upgrades for homes, buildings and site retrofits through the home energy long program.
Next slide. Finally, thrive. A guide for adjust transition supports the implementation of the playbooks by embedding these guiding principles into all our actions.
Climate change disproportionately impacts those who are already underserved. With intentional action, the benefits of climate change can be shared by all in our community.
Climate action can also position our community for success and rapidly evolving economy. The strategy identifies opportunities to operate more efficiently, reduce cost of managed future risks.
Climate action and reconciliation share a common goal to transform systems that perpetuate harm. The strategy supports community relations, resilience and well-being. Next slide.
Implementation and future planning will make use of an adaptive approach for a dynamic and flexible strategy to remain responsive to new challenges and opportunities.
I will note that approval of the strategy does not include approval of funding for initiatives outlined within the strategy.
Each of the initiatives will be evaluated and brought forward through budget deliberations for funding consideration and approval.
In conclusion, as a roadmap to reduce carbon pollution and improve climate resilience, the climate action strategy is fundamentally a risk management and fiscal stewardship tool.
Through decisive steps and clear initiatives, the strategy is a playbook to guide a safer, healthier and more prosperous future for Saskatoon. Thank you.
